subject: brain
topic: Teenagers are not lazy in the morning; their clocks run late
angle: While some evidence links later school start times to longer sleep and better outcomes, the quality of the research is often low or the results are limited by bias.
title: The biological cost of early starts

hooks.text: Is your school schedule hurting your sleep?
You think later starts help. The research is unclear.

A dark room and a glowing screen.

reveal.headline: The data on school start times is unreliable.
reveal.body: While some studies link later start times to better sleep, the quality of this evidence is very low due to a high risk of bias.

explain.headline: Sleep duration varies by schedule.
explain.body: Students in morning shifts have significantly higher rates of reduced sleep. Almost 80% of morning-shift students had average weekly sleep of less than 8 hours.

matters.headline: Your schedule may dictate your biology.
matters.body: That may be why you feel constant fatigue. The evidence suggests a link between later start times and improved sleep, but the results remain inconsistent.

example.headline: The alarm clock on the nightstand.
example.body: You stare at the ceiling in a dark room. The light from your phone shows the time. You feel heavy and tired before your day begins.

question.headline: Is your schedule working against your body?

claims.text: Later school start times are linked to better overall developmental outcomes, longer sleep duration, and less negative mood.
claims.quote: There is converging evidence that later SSTs are associated with better overall developmental outcomes, longer sleep duration, and less negative mood.

claims.text: The quality of the body of evidence regarding the effects of later school start times is very low because most studies were rated as being at high or unclear risk of bias.
claims.quote: Overall, the quality of the body of evidence was very low, as we rated most studies as being at high or unclear risk of bias with respect to allocation, attrition, absence of randomization, and the collection of baseline data.

claims.text: Reduced sleep duration was significantly higher in morning-shift students than in afternoon-shift students.
claims.quote: Reduced sleep duration was significantly higher in morning-shift students.

claims.text: The prevalence of reduced sleep durations (average weekly sleep duration, SDweek <8 h) was higher in morning-shift students (almost 80%) than in afternoon-shift ones (34%).
claims.quote: the prevalence of reduced sleep durations (average weekly sleep duration, SDweek <8 h) to be higher in morning-shift students (almost 80%) than in afternoon-shift ones (34%).

claims.text: Later school start times are linked to lower levels of sleepiness for high school youth compared to middle school youth.
claims.quote: Later SSTs were more strongly associated with lower levels of sleepiness for high school (versus middle school) youth

claims.text: Later school start times promoted longer sleep duration over 1 week in one study, but that study had a high risk of bias.
claims.quote: Later school start times promoted longer sleep duration over 1 week (1 study, high risk of bias).

verdict: The evidence suggests a link between later school start times and improved sleep for adolescents, but the data is inconsistent and often of low quality.
caveat: Many of the studies cited have a high or uncertain risk of bias, making it difficult to be confident about the actual effects of later school start times.
caption:
Your morning routine might be a biological mismatch.

Research suggests a link between later school start times and better sleep, but the evidence is often of low quality and shows high risk of bias.
